name: Ahashtari
title: Descendant of Judah through Ashhur
summary: Ahashtari is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:6 as the son of Ashhur, founder of Tekoa, and his wife Naara. He belongs to the tribe of Judah and is known exclusively from the genealogy. Although no events or deeds are linked to him personally, his place in the family tree testifies to the careful recording of Judah's descendants—an effort that served to preserve God's people's identity, inheritance rights, and continuity of promise throughout history.
roles: Ancestor in the tribe of Judah

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Judah's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Ahashtari is mentioned as one of the sons of Ashhur and Naara in the genealogy of Judah's descendants. Ashhur, called father of Tekoa, had two wives—Hela and Naara—and Naara bore Ahashtari among others.

keyEvents.title: The context of the genealogies in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Ahashtari is part of the extensive genealogies compiled to document the history and continuity of the tribe of Judah. These records were significant for tribal identity, inheritance rights, and service in the temple after the exile.

versions.summary: Ahashtari is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a descendant of Judah through the line of Ashhur. He is known only from the genealogies in the Books of Chronicles, and there is little information about his life beyond his place in the tribe of Judah.
versions.title: Descendant of Judah
versions.reason: [major] Ahazariah belongs to the genealogy of Judah in Chronicles, but he is not a patriarch. He fits better in a later period. Based on the context of the genealogies (descendants of Judah through Ashhur, father of Tekoa), he likely dates to the time of the judges or the early monarchy. 'judges' or 'united-kingdom' are more appropriate. Since Tekoa is known as a town in Judah associated with the period around the kingdom, 'united-kingdom' is a reasonable choice.; [minor] The roles array is empty. Even for a person known only from genealogies, it should at least include a role such as 'Descendant of Judah' or 'Ancestor in the tribe of Judah'.; [minor] The four key events are somewhat overlapping and repetitive for someone mentioned in just one verse. The third and fourth events concern context more than Ahazariah himself. They could be simplified to two events.; [minor] The scripture references 1 Chron 4:1-6 are too broad for the event 'Part of the tribe of Judah'. Ahazariah is specifically mentioned only in verse 6.; [minor] The fourth event includes 1 Chron 2:3-5 as a reference, but these verses concern Judah's sons generally and have no direct connection to Ahazariah.; [minor] The summary is acceptable but could be improved with a more precise formulation stating that Ahazariah is mentioned in 1 Chron 4:6.

He is known only from the genealogies in the Books of Chronicles and belongs to the tribe of Judah. Beyond his place in the family register, there are no further details about his life or deeds.

footnotes.text: The name Ahashtari (Hebrew: אֲחַשְׁתָּרִי, 'Aḥashtari') may possibly mean "belonging to Ashtar" or be connected to a place name. Some scholars have suggested a link with the Semitic goddess Ishtar/Ashtarte, which could indicate that the name originally had a cultural or geographical reference rather than a religious confession.

Ashhur is called "father of Tekoa" (1 Chron 4:5), an expression that likely means he was the founder or prominent leader in the town of Tekoa. Tekoa was located in the hill country of Judah, about 16 km south of Jerusalem, and is known as the hometown of the prophet Amos and the wise woman sent to David by Joab (2 Sam 14).

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 1–9 were likely compiled after the Babylonian exile to confirm the identity and inheritance rights of the returning Jews. These lists had practical significance for property rights, temple service, and tribal affiliation, and emphasized God's faithfulness through the generations.

In rabbinic tradition, there is little separate treatment of Ahashtari, but the genealogies in the Books of Chronicles were considered important for tracing messianic lineages and maintaining the identity of the tribes in Israel after the exile.
